questions.stem: A Windows workstation is set to obtain an IP address automatically, but no DHCP server responds. Which address range will Windows self-assign, and what is the practical limitation?

choices.text: 10.0.0.x; can reach the internet through NAT
169.254.x.x (APIPA); local-network only, no internet
192.168.0.x; only valid for guest networks
172.16.x.x; works only on Windows Server

questions.explanation: When DHCP fails, Windows self-assigns an APIPA address in the 169.254.x.x range. APIPA addresses only talk to other devices on the local network.
questions.trap: Other private ranges (10.x, 172.16-31.x, 192.168.x) are RFC1918 internal ranges, not APIPA. APIPA is specifically 169.254.

questions.stem: When configuring a static IPv4 address on Windows, which FOUR settings does the transcript list as required?

choices.text: MAC address, hostname, gateway, WINS server
Public IP, private IP, subnet mask, NAT type
IP address, subnet mask, default gateway, DNS server
SSID, WPA key, gateway, DNS

questions.explanation: A static IPv4 needs four pieces: IP address, subnet mask, default gateway (router), and DNS server (name resolver).
questions.trap: MAC address and SSID are device or wireless settings, not part of static IP configuration.

questions.stem: What does a VPN do for a remote employee on a coffee-shop Wi-Fi network?

choices.text: Creates a secure encrypted tunnel through the unsecured public network to the corporate VPN concentrator
Speeds up the public Wi-Fi connection by compressing all traffic
Disables the local firewall while connected
Replaces the device's MAC address with the corporate router's MAC

questions.explanation: A VPN creates a secure, encrypted tunnel for data to travel through an unsecured public network, terminating at a corporate VPN concentrator.
questions.trap: VPNs do not speed up a connection; encryption and tunneling overhead can actually slow it down.

questions.stem: Which is a correctly formatted UNC path to the share 'finance' on server 'fileserver01'?

choices.text: fileserver01:/finance
//fileserver01/finance
smb://fileserver01@finance
\\fileserver01\finance

questions.explanation: Windows UNC paths use the form \\server\share. So '\\fileserver01\finance' is correct.
questions.trap: Forward slashes are Linux/Mac style; on Windows UNC is double backslash plus backslash.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly contrasts a workgroup with an Active Directory domain?

choices.text: Workgroup is a corporate central-management model; domain is a decentralized peer model
Workgroup is decentralized (each computer manages itself); domain is centralized via Active Directory
Both are identical, just named differently in Home vs Pro
Workgroups require a Windows Server; domains do not

questions.explanation: A workgroup is decentralized - each PC manages its own accounts. A domain is centralized through Active Directory Domain Services.
questions.trap: The trap reverses it: domains REQUIRE a server running AD; workgroups do not.

questions.stem: A remote user is tethering to a cellular hotspot with limited data. Which Windows setting should be enabled on that connection to reduce data usage?

choices.text: Metered connection
APIPA fallback
Mapped drive
Static DNS

questions.explanation: Enabling a metered connection tells Windows to reduce background data usage on that interface to avoid surprise charges on pay-per-use networks.
questions.trap: APIPA is a fallback addressing behavior, not a data-saving setting.

questions.stem: Windows Defender Firewall picks different rule sets based on the network profile. Which statement is correct?

choices.text: Private networks default to the highest security; Public networks default to permissive
Both profiles share identical rules by default
There is no distinction between Public and Private profiles
Public networks default to the highest security; Private networks are treated as trusted

questions.explanation: Public profile applies the strictest rules by default (assume hostile coffee-shop Wi-Fi). Private profile treats home/work as trusted.
questions.trap: The reversed claim (Private strictest, Public permissive) is the trap; remember Public = strictest, Private = trusted.

questions.stem: A user wants to access \\fs01\projects as drive letter S: every time they sign in. Which Windows feature does this?

choices.text: Static IP
A mapped drive
DHCP reservation
Metered connection

questions.explanation: Mapping a drive assigns a drive letter (e.g. S:) to a UNC path on a server, so the user opens 'S:' instead of typing \\fs01\projects every time.
questions.trap: DHCP reservations are about IPs, not about share access.

questions.stem: In a corporate network, what does a proxy server do for the client's web traffic?

choices.text: Acts as a middleman that fetches web pages on the user's behalf, often inspecting for safety
Encrypts all storage on the local disk
Replaces the DHCP server
Provides time synchronization for Active Directory

questions.explanation: A proxy server sits between the client and the web, fetching pages and (often) inspecting them for safety before returning them.
questions.trap: VPNs encrypt traffic end-to-end; proxies broker traffic and filter, which is a different role.

questions.stem: Which wireless security setup is correct per the transcript?

choices.text: Use WEP with TKIP for modern Wi-Fi
Disable SSID broadcast as the primary security control
Use WPA2 or WPA3 with AES encryption
Open networks are fine as long as the firewall is on

questions.explanation: Modern Wi-Fi should use WPA2 or WPA3 with AES encryption.
questions.trap: WEP is obsolete and TKIP is the legacy WPA1 cipher; do not pair them for modern networks.
